title: Are Our Schools Humane?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart voices a question that has nagged him for months: are schools humane places? He opens with three vignettes: a colleague in tears over the personal cost of professional dedication, a bored student who would rather stay in a program he dislikes than check a vague rumor about a better one, and a sobbing student crushed by school stress and her parents' zero-tolerance rules. He then borrows Peter Drucker's lifelong question, how to make society both more productive and more humane, and turns it on schools. His claim is that systems have sacrificed humanity to productivity for so long that we barely remember what being human means, and that chasing scores alone is chasing the wind. He closes by redirecting attention from mere scores to producing mature people capable of flourishing lives.
points: Drucker's question about making society both productive and humane is a useful test for schools as well as workplaces.
The vignettes show concrete human costs, from teacher overwork to student stress and sleep loss, that productivity metrics hide.
Doing less but better is a theme that recurs in the research on well-led careers, though it is bitter for American teachers carrying heavy contact hours and testing pressure.
Stuart argues schools should aim at mature human beings able to build flourishing lives, not merely at higher scores.
quotes: There’s a question that’s been nagging at me for months and months, starting at the end of last school year, persisting at times through the summer, and now louder and clearer with a new school year under way. It’s been a hard one for me to voice because I’m keen on focusing on what I can control and keeping an eye on the bright side.

It’s amazing how much of the research and wisdom on living the well-led life (and building the well-led career) sings to the harmony of doing less but better. It’s one of those hard candy truisms — you mull them over, work at them, relish them for a long time rather than chomping into them in one bite.

Another student, this one sobbing. She’s overwhelmed by the stress of school and by her parents’ stress of school. They want her to do well, so they require that she not have zeroes in any of her classes.
All of it’s an escape,” she sniffles. “I know that. But sometimes it’s just nice to get away from this pressure, from being forced to take all these classes. I just want to get a job and be done.

Did you do what I did — automatically turn Drucker’s question toward our schools? And I can’t help but react with a fallen face. It’s not just that we seem more and more accustomed to sacrificing our humanity on the altar of productivity.
So let us face the brutal facts. Drucker is right: when we pursue the productivity of our schools without keeping in view their humanity, we chase the wind at great expense.
